title: Reformed confess inherent justice and a secondary formal sense
source_text: XXVII. Atque inde est quod Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, existimantes nos ejusmodi monstra sub doctrina de imputatione justitiae Christi tegere & alere, illam tam acriter impugnant. Sed, quam ab eo simus alieni ex vera & genuina sententiae nostrae expositione manifestum fecimus. Siquidem ultro confitemur, & eum qui justificatur simul intus a peccatis per Spiritum Sanctum mundari, & fidelibus infundi justitiam inhaerentem, qua interius renoventur, & in se justi fiant. Neque dicimus fideles apud Deum pro mundis, piis & justis censeri, licet in se impii & immundi maneant, sed illos revera pios, mundos, & sanctos per Spiritus Sancti gratiam fieri: Multa quoque eorum opera agnoscimus pia, sancta & justa esse, non simpliciter spurca & immunda, atque adeo peccata mortalia. Ac denique praeter justificationem illam judiciariam, quam ad solum Christi meritum & justitiam referimus, quamque constituimus in absolutione a reatu mortis & perditionis, quam legem Dei violando, apud severum ejus tribunal commeriti sumus, fatemur cum Davenantio, de Just. habituali, c. 21. Damus quandam, ut ita loquamur, justificationem, cujus causam formalem justitiam nobis inhaerentem dici non improbamus. Et cum Theologis Polonis, in sua Confessione, cap. 4. Non negamus etiam dici posse fideles per charitatem aliasque virtutes infusas justificari, id est, justos effici & censeri.
pass_a_gloss: And thence it is that the doctors of the Roman Church, thinking we hide and foster such monsters under the doctrine of the imputation of Christ’s righteousness, attack it so fiercely. But how far we are from that we have made plain from a true and genuine exposition of our judgment. For we freely confess that he who is justified is at the same time inwardly cleansed from sins by the Holy Spirit, and that inherent righteousness is infused in the faithful by which they are inwardly renewed and made just in themselves. Nor do we say that the faithful are reckoned before God as clean, pious, and just while they remain in themselves impious and unclean, but that they truly become pious, clean, and holy by the Holy Spirit’s grace. We also acknowledge many of their works to be pious, holy, and just—not simply filthy and unclean and thus mortal sins. And finally, besides that judicial justification which we refer to Christ’s merit and righteousness alone, and which we constitute in absolution from the guilt of death and perdition which we have deserved at his severe tribunal by violating God’s law, we confess with Davenant (On Habitual Justice, ch. 21) that we grant a certain justification, so to speak, whose formal cause we do not disapprove of calling the righteousness inhering in us. And with the Polish theologians in their Confession, chapter 4: We do not deny that the faithful can also be said to be justified—that is, made and reckoned just—by charity and other infused virtues.
pass_b_english: Rome fights a monster we do not teach: we confess Spirit-cleansing and infused inherent justice.
Besides forensic absolution we allow with Davenant/Poles a secondary formal justification by inherent virtue.
